p: Ben Sira takes up a warning from Proverbs about drink and poverty.
b: The verse goes with 18:32-33, where the reader is told not to throw feasts on borrowed money. Proverbs gives the same warning: "For the drunkard and the glutton lose everything they have" (Proverbs 23:21). Ben Sira adds a second line about "small things": a person who despises small savings, or small faults, slides downhill without noticing. The Greek kata mikron, "little by little", is the slow fall the line describes.

p: Paul uses the very participle that Ben Sira's grandson used here.
b: The Greek ho kollōmenos pornais, "the one who joins himself to prostitutes", is the phrase Paul uses in the singular: "the man who joins himself to a prostitute is one body with her" (1 Corinthians 6:16). The verb means to glue or bind closely, and the Greek of Genesis 2:24 uses a compound of it for a man joined to his wife. Ben Sira's point is practical: such a man "grows more reckless". Paul's point is about the body that belongs to Christ. Whether Paul knew Sirach here cannot be shown; the shared phrase may simply be common Jewish Greek.

p: A picture of the grave, not of punishment after death.
b: Worms in the grave are a stock picture of death in the Bible: "Under you, maggots make your mattress; / worms are your bedcovers" (Isaiah 14:11). Ben Sira uses it again at 10:11. Judith 16:17 and Mark 9:48 take the image further, to the fate of the wicked after judgment, but Ben Sira says only that the reckless man ends in decay. "Will inherit him" is ironic: the man who wasted his inheritance becomes an inheritance for worms.

a: unless your silence would make you guilty
p: The Greek says only 'unless it is a sin for you': keeping a secret can itself be wrong.
b: Literally "if it is not a sin for you, do not uncover it". Ben Sira's rule is to keep what you hear to yourself, with one exception: when keeping quiet would make you guilty. The law of Moses names such a case: a witness who "hears the public curse calling for witnesses ... but he does not tell. Then he will carry his guilt" (Leviticus 5:1). The Plain spells out the sense so that the exception is not read as "if you have not sinned".

p: A fool cannot hold news in; it presses to get out like a baby.
b: The fool who has heard something is pictured as a woman in labor: the word has to come out, and the pressure is unbearable. Elihu uses a similar picture of words he cannot hold: "it is about to burst like new wineskins" (Job 32:19), and 19:10 has just told the reader, "you will not burst from it". The next verse turns the picture around: the word is an arrow stuck in the thigh, painful until it is pulled out.

t: The belly as the inner self
p: In Hebrew thought the belly is where hidden thoughts are kept.
b: The Greek koilia, "belly", stands for the inner self, as the Hebrew beten often does. Proverbs says a gossip's words "slide into the deepest rooms of the belly" (Proverbs 18:8). The Plain keeps the bodily word so that the picture of an arrow lodged in the thigh, a wound that will not let a man rest, stays sharp.

a: Take it up with your friend
t: 'Take it up with': one Greek verb, four times
p: The verb means to question, test or correct; the same word stands in Leviticus 19:17 and Matthew 18:15.
b: The Greek elenxon opens 19:13, 14, 15 and 17. It covers asking, testing the facts and correcting, so the Plain uses "take it up with", which does not assume the friend is guilty ("maybe he did not do it"). The KJV has "Admonish". The Greek of Leviticus 19:17 uses the same verb: "Be sure to correct your fellow citizen, so that you do not carry sin because of him" (Leviticus 19:17). Jesus uses it too: "go and correct him, with just the two of you there" (Matthew 18:15). Elsewhere in these chapters the noun is "rebuke" or "correction" (20:1-2; 21:6).

p: The Greek diabolē is the word from which 'devil' (diabolos, 'slanderer') comes.
b: Diabolē means a false charge, slander. The New Testament's diabolos, "the devil", is the slanderer, the one who brings false charges. Ben Sira's reason for checking a story with a friend is that most such stories are slander. The rest of the verse echoes Proverbs: "A naive person trusts every word he hears" (Proverbs 14:15). The Greek of that proverb has the same words, pisteuei panti logō, "believes every word".

a: Is there anyone whose tongue has never made him sin?
p: James says the same: all of us trip up in what we say.
b: Ben Sira excuses the friend who "slips, but not from the heart": a hasty word is not the same as a planned lie. The question that follows assumes the answer "no one". James puts it this way: "All of us trip up in many ways. Whoever never trips in what he says is a complete man" (James 3:2). Ben Sira returns to the dangers of the tongue in 20:18 and in the prayer of 22:27.

p: Ben Sira's favorite title for God, Greek hypsistos.
b: Ho hypsistos, "the Most High", translates the Hebrew 'Elyon, the title of God in Genesis 14:18-22 and the Psalms. Ben Sira uses it often. "Make room for the law of the Most High" means: let the law decide, instead of your anger. Leviticus 19:17-18 joins the duty to correct a neighbor with the ban on revenge and the command to love him, which is the law Ben Sira has in mind.

p: This added line hopes for immortality, which the base text of Ben Sira does not promise.
b: The line is found only in the longer Greek text (see the variant). It speaks of "the tree of immortality", recalling the tree of life (Genesis 2:9; Revelation 2:7). The shorter Greek and the Hebrew of Ben Sira do not hold out life after death: in 17:27-28 the dead cannot praise God, and "in Hades no one argues over the length of a life" (41:4). The added line goes beyond the base text and is closer to Wisdom 3:1-4 and to the New Testament hope. Churches that read the longer text, as the KJV does, find that hope here; most modern translations put the line in a footnote.

a: All wisdom is the fear of the Lord
t: Wisdom and the fear of the Lord
p: The book's main theme, in Proverbs' words: wisdom begins with reverence for God.
b: This is the thesis of the whole book, stated at length in 1:11-30. Proverbs says, "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7), and Job, "the fear of the Lord is wisdom" (Job 28:28). Ben Sira adds that wisdom always includes doing the law. In these chapters the theme comes back at 21:11 and 23:27, framing the practical advice: good manners, silence and loyalty are wisdom only when they grow out of reverence for God.

a: Better to fall short in understanding and fear God
p: A simple person who fears God is better off than a brilliant one who breaks the law.
b: Ben Sira was a scholar who loved learning (38:24-39:11), yet he ranks reverence above intelligence. The Greek emphobos, "full of fear", means fearing God. Brilliance that breaks the law is worse than plain faithfulness. Christian readers have often set the verse beside 1 Corinthians 1:20-25, where God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, though Paul's point is about the cross, not about the law.

p: The Greek can mean bending the truth to get a verdict, or abusing a favor.
b: Diastrephōn charin tou ekphanai krima. If charin is the preposition "for the sake of", the line means "one who twists things in order to bring a verdict to light", either a lawyer who bends the facts or a clever judge who uses tricks to bring out the truth. If charin is the noun "favor", it means "one who perverts a favor to win a verdict". The Plain takes the first. The longer Greek adds a third line, "and there is a wise man who gives a right judgment" (see the variant).

p: Dark clothes and a bowed head were signs of mourning and fasting, easy to fake.
b: The Greek melania, "blackness", is mourning dress or a gloomy look, and "bowed low" is the posture of grief or penitence. The scoundrel uses the outward signs of piety as a disguise. Jesus warns against the same show: "When you fast, do not take on a gloomy look like the hypocrites" (Matthew 6:16). Isaiah 58:5 mocks a fast in which a man "hangs his head like a bulrush" (Isaiah 58:5).

a: acts as if he were deaf
p: A rare Greek word: pretending not to hear.
b: Heterokōphōn joins "one of two" and "deaf": deaf in one ear, that is, deaf when it suits him. The longer Greek has ethelokōphōn, "deaf by choice". The man keeps his eyes down and his ears closed so that he seems harmless, but "where no one knows him", away from people who would see through him, he strikes first. Compare the enemy of 12:16, who weeps with his eyes while planning harm.

p: Ben Sira trusts outward signs; other passages warn that appearances deceive.
b: 19:26-28 have just described a man whose looks hide deceit, and now 19:29-30 say a man is known by his look, his clothes, his laugh and his walk. The two fit together: a careful observer can see through the act, because habits show. The Bible also warns against judging by looks: "the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Ben Sira speaks of reading character; Samuel speaks of God's choice.

p: Chapter 20 is built from short paired sayings that begin 'there is'.
b: Most of 20:1-23 is made of sayings that begin estin, "there is": there is a rebuke ..., there is silence ..., there is a gift .... The Hebrew of MS C, where it survives (20:5-6, 22-23), begins them with yesh, "there is", the same pattern. The form sets two cases side by side so that the reader learns to tell them apart: two silences, two gifts, two kinds of shame. Ecclesiastes 3:1-8 uses a similar method with "a time to ...".

p: Forced justice is like a eunuch's desire: violent and impotent at once.
b: The comparison is meant to shock. A eunuch may want a young woman but cannot have her; if he tries, he can only do violence. So with a judge or ruler who "tries to bring about justice by force": violence cannot produce what justice is meant to produce. Ben Sira uses the same picture at 30:20 for a sick man who cannot enjoy good food. Deuteronomy 22:25-27 treats the forcing of a young woman as a crime like murder, so the image also tells the reader how ugly forced justice is.

a: One person keeps quiet and turns out to be wise
p: Proverbs said even a fool seems wise if he stays silent; Ben Sira splits the case in two.
b: "Even a stubborn fool, if he stays silent, is counted as wise" (Proverbs 17:28). Ben Sira looks closer: one person keeps quiet because he has nothing to say, another because he is waiting for the right moment (20:6). The Hebrew of MS C reads "is counted wise", closer to Proverbs, where the Greek has "is found wise". "A time to keep quiet and a time to speak" (Ecclesiastes 3:7) is the rule both chapters apply.

p: The Greek lapistēs is a boaster; a corrector of Vaticanus wrote 'liar' in the margin.
b: Lapistēs is a rare word for a swaggering talker. In Codex Vaticanus a later hand noted pseustēs, "liar", in the margin, as Swete reports. The Hebrew of MS C has only one figure, the kesil, the fool of Proverbs: "but a fool does not watch for the time". The Greek "will run past the moment" says the same: he speaks too soon and misses the right time.

a: his eyes are many instead of one
p: A fool gives one thing and looks for many back.
b: The Greek is brief: "his eyes are many instead of one". The fool watches his one gift with many eyes, expecting much in return. The longer Greek spells it out, "his eyes are many instead of one, to receive" (see the variant), and the KJV follows it: "he looketh to receive many things for one". 20:15-16 show what happens when the return does not come: he complains to everyone that no one thanks him.
orig: οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ ἀνθ᾽ ἑνὸς πολλοί

p: The herald cried public news in the streets; the stingy giver broadcasts his gifts.
b: A kēryx, "herald", made public announcements in Greek cities and in royal courts. The man who gives a little makes sure everyone hears about it, then calls his loan back the next day. Jesus warns against the same show: when you give, "do not have a trumpet blown ahead of you" (Matthew 6:2).

a: Those who eat at my table speak ill of me
p: The fool's complaint borrows the words of Psalm 41 about a friend's betrayal.
b: Literally "those who eat my bread are worthless with the tongue". Eating someone's bread made you his friend and guest. The Psalm says, "the one I trusted, / who ate my bread, / has raised his heel high against me" (Psalm 41:9), and Jesus applies it to Judas (John 13:18). In Ben Sira the complaint is the fool's own: he has no friends because his gifts were never really gifts (20:14-15).

a: Better to lose your footing on the floor than with your tongue
p: A fall on the floor bruises; a slip of the tongue can ruin.
b: The comparison is between a fall on a smooth floor and a fall caused by careless words. Ben Sira returns to it in 22:27 and 28:26. James says the tongue is "a fire" (James 3:6). The second line warns that the downfall of evil people comes just as suddenly as a slip.

p: Paideia and its family are 'discipline' in this part: training that shapes, including correction.
b: The Greek root paid- runs through these chapters: paideia "discipline" (19:19; 21:19, 21; 22:6; 23:2, 7), paideuō "discipline" (21:12; 23:15), apaideutos "undisciplined" (20:19, 24; 22:3), apaideusia "lack of discipline" (21:24; 22:10; 23:13) and pepaideumenos "disciplined" (21:23). The word means the training of a child or a pupil, by teaching and, where needed, by punishment. The Plain keeps one English root so the reader can follow it; in 22:6 and 23:2 the whip is close by. Proverbs uses Hebrew musar the same way, "discipline" on this site.

a: A proverb is rejected when it comes from a fool's mouth
t: A proverb in a fool's mouth
p: Proverbs 26:7 and 26:9 say a proverb in a fool's mouth is useless or dangerous.
b: Twice Proverbs ends a saying with "and a proverb in fools' mouths" (Proverbs 26:7; 26:9): limp like a lame man's legs, or harmful like a thorn in a drunkard's hand. Ben Sira gives the reason: a fool "never says it at the right time". A true saying spoken at the wrong moment is still a wrong word. The Greek parabolē is the Septuagint's word for a proverb, and the New Testament's word for a parable.

a: Lying is a foul stain on a person
p: Three verses on lies: a stain, worse than theft, a shame that stays.
b: Ben Sira ranks a habitual liar below a thief (20:25), because a thief takes goods but a liar destroys trust. Proverbs says, "Lips that lie are abhorrent to the LORD" (Proverbs 12:22), and the ninth commandment forbids lying testimony (Exodus 20:16). The refrain "it will always be in the mouths of the undisciplined" repeats 20:19 word for word in the Greek, and the Plain repeats it too.

a: The wise will move ahead by what they say
p: Codex Vaticanus has the title 'Sayings in proverbs' here; the Plain shows it as the heading.
b: At the end of 20:26 Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, has the words Logoi parabolōn, "Sayings in proverbs" or "Words of parables". They are a section title, not part of the verse, and the Plain uses them as the heading above 20:27. The Greek manuscripts of Sirach carry several such titles (18:30 "Self-control"; 23:7 "Discipline for the mouth"). The longer text of codex 248 has the same title here. They show how ancient readers divided the book.

t: Smoothing over a wrong at court
p: The verb is the Bible's word for making atonement; here it means appeasing a powerful man.
b: Exilasetai adikian, literally "will make atonement for injustice". The verb is the Greek Old Testament's word for the Hebrew kipper, "make atonement". The Greek of Proverbs 16:14 uses it of the wise man who calms a king's fury ("but a wise man will calm it"). Here it describes court life: a man in favor with the powerful can smooth over a wrong. Ben Sira states this as a fact of life; 20:29 at once warns that gifts to the powerful blind them. The same verb says almsgiving atones for sins in 3:30.

a: blind the eyes of the wise
p: Ben Sira quotes the law of Moses on bribes.
b: Deuteronomy says, "a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and turns the words of the righteous upside down" (Deuteronomy 16:19), and Exodus 23:8 says the same. Ben Sira widens it: even "guest gifts", xenia, the presents given to visitors and officials, can silence the honest rebuke a wise man owes. The muzzle is the gag that keeps a wise counselor from speaking.

p: Ben Sira repeats these two verses at 41:14-15; Jesus' sayings about the lamp and the talent make the same point.
b: 20:30-31 come back almost word for word at 41:14-15 in the Greek. Wisdom is meant to be used for others; a sage who keeps it to himself is like a man who buries his money. Jesus says no one lights a lamp "only to set it under a grain basket" (Matthew 5:15), and the servant who "hid your talent in the ground" (Matthew 25:25) is condemned. Ben Sira still prefers a hidden fool to a hidden sage (20:31): folly is better kept out of sight.

p: The Greek says 'child'; the Hebrew of Ben Sira, where it survives, says 'my son'.
b: Teknon is "child". Where the Hebrew of Ben Sira survives, the teacher's address is beni, "my son" (for example in Kahana's text of 3:12 and 4:1), as in Proverbs (Proverbs 1:8). The Hebrew of 21:1 is lost. "Son" reflects the school, where the pupils were young men (51:23); the grandson's "child" fits any reader. The Plain follows the Greek.

a: Do not do it any more
p: The first remedy for sin is to stop; the second is to pray about the past.
b: Ben Sira does not tell the sinner to despair or to pretend. He gives two steps: stop, and pray for forgiveness of the sins already done. Jesus sends the woman away with the same command: "Go, and from now on, do not keep on sinning" (John 8:11; compare John 5:14). Ben Sira's teaching on repentance runs through the book (5:5-7; 17:24-29; 18:21).

a: as you would from a snake
t: Sin as a snake and a lion
p: Two animal pictures of sin: the snake that bites and the lion that kills.
b: Sin is pictured as an animal that attacks whoever comes close. Genesis 4:7 pictures sin "crouching at the door", and the snake of Genesis 3 lies behind the first picture. The lion's teeth recall Psalm 58:6 and Joel 1:6. The New Testament uses the lion for the devil, who "is walking about like a lion that roars" (1 Peter 5:8). Ben Sira's advice is not to fight it but to run, as Paul says of sexual sin (1 Corinthians 6:18).

a: a sword that cuts both ways
p: The Greek 'two-mouthed sword' is the same word as in Hebrews 4:12.
b: Rhomphaia distomos, literally "a two-mouthed sword", a blade sharp on both edges. Proverbs says the strange woman's end is "as sharp as a sword that cuts both ways" (Proverbs 5:4), and the Plain uses the same English. Hebrews uses the same adjective of God's word: "It cuts deeper than any sword with two edges" (Hebrews 4:12). In Ben Sira the sword is lawlessness, and its wound has no cure.

p: The Greek says only 'his ears'; almost all readers take them to be God's.
b: The Greek is heōs ōtiōn autou, "to his ears". Grammatically the ears could be the poor man's own, but the second line, "the verdict for him comes swiftly", shows that a judge is hearing, and the KJV reads "to the ears of God". The Plain names God so the line is not misread. The thought is the law's: "he cries out to me, be sure I will hear his cry" (Exodus 22:23). James says the cry of cheated workers "gone into the ears of the Lord of Armies" (James 5:4).

p: Tow, the waste fiber of flax, catches fire at once.
b: Stippyon is tow, the short fibers left when flax is combed. It burns in a flash. Isaiah uses it of the strong man who "will turn into flax fiber" (Isaiah 1:31), and Judges 16:9 says Samson broke his cords "as a strand of tow breaks at a whiff of fire" (Judges 16:9). A gang of lawless men may look strong, bound together, but their end is fire.

a: made smooth and clear of stones
t: A smooth road to the pit
p: The Greek may mean cleared of stones or paved with stones; either way the road is easy.
b: Hōmalismenē ek lithōn. With ek, "out of", the road is leveled and cleared of stones; the longer Greek has hypo lithōn, "by stones", which the KJV renders "made plain with stones", that is, paved. Both make the same point: sin's road is easy walking. "There is a road that looks straight to a person, / but in the end it comes out on the roads of death" (Proverbs 14:12). Compare Jesus' wide road "that leads to ruin" (Matthew 7:13).

p: Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead; Ben Sira does not describe torment there.
b: Bothros hadou, "the pit of Hades". In the Greek Old Testament Hades translates Sheol, the place of all the dead. For Ben Sira it is the end of life, a place where no one praises God (17:27-28) and where it no longer matters how long a life was (41:4); he does not describe punishment there. Later Jewish and Christian readers, who believed in judgment after death, could read the road to "the pit of Hades" as the road to hell, as in Jesus' wide road "that leads to ruin" (Matthew 7:13).

a: gets the upper hand over his thoughts
p: Later rabbis said God made the evil inclination and gave the Torah as its cure.
b: Ben Sira says keeping the law gives a man control of his ennoēma, his thoughts and intentions. In 15:14 he says God left humanity in the hand of its diaboulion, the inclination the Hebrew calls yetser. The Talmud later puts the idea this way: God says, "I created an evil inclination, ... and I created Torah as its antidote" (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 30b). The verse and the rabbinic saying share one conviction: the law trains the inner life, not only outward acts. Genesis 4:7 ("you must rule over it") is the text the Talmud cites.

p: Panourgia is good sense in Proverbs, but here Ben Sira shows its dark side too.
b: Panourgia literally means "readiness to do anything". The Greek of Proverbs uses it for the good sense the naive need: "to give shrewdness to the innocent" (Proverbs 1:4 in the Greek), and the shrewd person of Proverbs 14:15 is panourgos. Ben Sira uses it both ways: no one can be taught without some shrewdness, but there is a shrewdness that only makes things bitter (also 19:25). The Plain uses "shrewd" throughout (21:20; 22:27) so the reader can follow the word.

p: The wise man's advice is the spring of life of Proverbs 13:14.
b: "The teaching of the wise is a spring of life" (Proverbs 13:14). The flood of the first line is an image of abundance, the spring of the second an image of something that never runs dry. The fool of the next verse is the opposite: a cracked jar that holds nothing.

p: A fool cannot keep knowledge, as a broken jar cannot keep water.
b: The Greek angeion syntetrimmenon is a broken or cracked vessel. Jeremiah used the image of Israel's false gods: "cisterns full of cracks / that do not hold the water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Ben Sira turns it on the fool's mind: whatever is poured in leaks out. The jar stands opposite the flood and the spring of 21:13.

p: A biblical idiom for rejecting something with contempt.
b: To throw something behind your back is to reject it and refuse to think about it. God says to Jeroboam, "me you threw behind your back" (1 Kings 14:9), and Nehemiah 9:26 says the people threw the law behind their backs. The man of knowledge "builds on" a wise word; the pleasure-lover throws it away.

p: Ben Sira's scribes spoke in public councils as well as in schools.
b: Ekklēsia here is the public gathering of the people or the town, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the assembly of Israel (Deuteronomy 31:30). Ben Sira pictures the sensible man as someone people seek out when decisions are made. Later he says craftsmen are not sought out in the assembly (38:33), while the scribe serves among the great (39:4). Proverbs 5:14 shows the assembly as a place of public judgment; 23:24 shows that side of it too.

p: The same discipline feels like chains to the fool and like jewelry to the sensible.
b: 21:19 and 21:21 are a matched pair: to the thoughtless, discipline is shackles on the feet and handcuffs on the right hand; to the sensible, it is a gold ornament and a band on the right arm. Proverbs says the teaching of parents "will be a charming wreath on your head / and a string of beads around your neck" (Proverbs 1:9). In 6:24-31 Ben Sira says the same of Wisdom: "her shackles will become a mighty shelter for you" (6:29), and "A gold ornament is on her" (6:30), the same Greek words as "gold ornament" here.

a: quick to go into a house
t: Do not walk into a house uninvited
p: The Talmud quotes 'the book of ben Sira' against entering another's house suddenly.
b: Proverbs advises, "Keep your visits to your neighbor's house rare" (Proverbs 25:17). Ben Sira adds manners: the fool walks straight in, peeks from the door and listens at it (21:23-24). The Babylonian Talmud (Niddah 16b) cites "the book of ben Sira" for a list of three people it hates and a fourth it does not love, and the fourth is "one who enters the house of another suddenly". That saying is not in the Greek; Kahana's Hebrew edition prints it after 21:22-23. Rabbi Yochanan there extends it even to one's own house.

p: The Greek of Vaticanus is obscure; other witnesses read 'tell' for 'grow heavy'.
b: Codex Vaticanus reads "The lips of strangers in these things will be heavy". Perhaps: busybodies, whose business it is not, are loaded down with talk about other people's affairs, while sensible people weigh every word. Codex Sinaiticus reads "will tell" for "will be heavy", and the longer Greek reads "The lips of chatterers will tell what is not theirs", which the KJV follows (see the variant). The verb "grow heavy" repeats 21:24 ("too heavy to bear"), and the scale of the second line plays on it.

p: Satan or 'the adversary'? Either way, the man who blames another is cursing himself.
b: The Greek ton satanan can be read three ways. (1) Satan, the devil: a sinner who curses the devil for tempting him really curses himself, since the choice was his own; Ben Sira has already forbidden blaming God for one's sins (15:11-12). (2) "The adversary" in the Hebrew sense, a human opponent, as Hadad was "an adversary for Solomon" (1 Kings 11:14): cursing an enemy brings the curse back on you. (3) The rabbis later said, "Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death are one" (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 16a, Reish Lakish); on that reading the ungodly man curses his own evil impulse, which is himself. The Hebrew of this verse is lost.

p: The whisperer is a gossip; Paul lists 'whisperers' among the sins of a godless world.
b: Ho psithyrizōn is the one who whispers about others behind their backs. Ben Sira warns against being called one (5:14) and calls a curse on him (28:13). Paul uses the related noun in his list: "They whisper behind backs" (Romans 1:29). Proverbs says "a gossip splits up the closest of friends" (Proverbs 16:28). Ben Sira's point is that the gossip stains himself first.

p: Ben Sira's word is the one the Greek Proverbs uses for the lazy one.
b: Oknēros is the word the Greek of Proverbs uses for the Hebrew 'atsel: "Go to the ant, you lazy one" (Proverbs 6:6). The Plain uses Proverbs' English. Proverbs mocks the lazy one with humor (Proverbs 26:13-15); Ben Sira uses disgust: a stone smeared with filth, a lump of dung. Hissing (22:1) was the gesture of scorn people made at a ruin (Jeremiah 19:8).

p: The Greek word is cattle dung, used in the ancient world as fuel and fertilizer.
b: Bolbiton is cow dung; the Latin has "the dung of oxen". It was a common sight in a village, collected from the manure pile and dried for fuel (compare Ezekiel 4:15). Anyone who picks up a fresh lump shakes it off his hand at once. So people react to the lazy one.

a: a daughter is born to his loss
p: Ben Sira speaks harshly of daughters; the Bible elsewhere calls children a gift.
b: The Greek says only "a daughter is born for loss". Read with the first line and with 22:4-5, it may mean a daughter like the undisciplined son, a shameful daughter, and the KJV supplies "a foolish daughter". Read alone, it says any daughter is a loss, and other passages show how Ben Sira saw daughters: a worry that robs a father of sleep (42:9-11), to be guarded closely (7:24; 26:10). Here he goes beyond the 66 books, which call children "an inheritance the LORD gives" (Psalm 127:3), give daughters inheritance (Numbers 27:8; Job 42:15) and praise the woman of strength (Proverbs 31:10-31). Churches that read Sirach as Scripture take such verses as the advice of a father in a culture where a daughter's honor was the family's, not as a judgment on women.

a: whippings and discipline are wisdom in every season
p: Ben Sira, like Proverbs, assumed physical punishment was part of raising and teaching children.
b: The Greek mastiges kai paideia, "whips and discipline", reflects the schools and homes of Ben Sira's time, where beating was normal. Proverbs says, "Whoever keeps back his rod hates his son" (Proverbs 13:24), and Ben Sira says more at 30:1-13. Readers today differ: some take these verses as a timeless command about physical discipline; others read them as the practice of an ancient culture, keeping the point that correction is love (Proverbs 3:12; Hebrews 12:5-11) while rejecting the rod. The topic page sets out the debate.

p: A Genizah manuscript preserves most of this verse in Hebrew, close to the Greek.
b: Genizah MS C, an anthology of Ben Sira's sayings, keeps this verse: "Over the dead weep, for his light has ceased; and over a fool weep, for understanding has ceased", and on the next lines, "... over the dead, for he is at rest ... than death, a bad life". The Greek hēdion, "more sweetly", means "less bitterly": the dead are at rest, but the fool's life is a living death. Codices A and C read idion, a spelling slip.

a: The dead are mourned for seven days
p: Seven days was the usual period of mourning, as in Genesis 50:10 and the later Jewish shiva.
b: "Joseph held seven days of mourning for his father" (Genesis 50:10). The people of Jabesh fasted seven days for Saul (1 Samuel 31:13), Job's friends sat seven days in silence (Job 2:13), and Israel mourned Judith seven days (Judith 16:24). Jewish practice still keeps seven days, shiva ("seven"). Ben Sira's twist: the fool needs mourning all his life. Elsewhere he advises keeping grief for the dead short, "for a day or two" (38:17).

a: his madness will not wear you out
p: The Greek verb is the root of acedia, the listless weariness later monks counted a deadly sin.
b: Akēdiasēs, "be worn out, weary, downcast". The noun akēdia became the Christian monks' name for the spiritual listlessness that makes prayer and work tasteless, one of the vices of the monastic lists. Ben Sira means something simpler: a fool's company drains you. The word for "madness", aponoia, means senselessness, loss of good judgment.

a: Sand and salt and a lump of iron
p: Ben Sira expands Proverbs 27:3 on the weight of a fool.
b: "A stone is heavy and sand weighs a lot, / but a stubborn fool's provoking is heavier than both" (Proverbs 27:3). Ben Sira turns it into a riddle: what is heavier than lead? Its name is "fool" (22:14). Then he lists heavy loads from daily life: sand, salt and iron. A person without understanding is harder to carry than any of them.

a: A wooden tie-beam built into a house
p: Builders laid wooden beams into stone walls to hold them together in an earthquake.
b: Himantōsis xylinē, "wooden binding": a timber beam laid into masonry. Solomon's builders set "three layers of cut stone and a layer of cedar beams" (1 Kings 6:36), and the same method appears in Ezra 6:4. Wood gives a stone wall flexibility when the ground shakes. So a heart bound together by well-thought-out counsel does not break when the moment of crisis comes.

a: telling a secret and a treacherous blow
p: Hot words can be forgiven; contempt, a betrayed secret and a stab in the back cannot.
b: Ben Sira separates quarrels from betrayal. A drawn sword or angry words leave a way back, but taunting, arrogance, a revealed secret and a treacherous blow drive any friend away. He says the same at 27:16-21: "Whoever tells secrets has ruined trust" (27:16). Proverbs warns, "do not spill a secret that belongs to someone else" (Proverbs 25:9), and contrasts honest wounds with false kisses (Proverbs 27:6).

p: Insults are the smoke that warns of violence to come.
b: Steam and smoke rise from a furnace before the flames break out. In the same way, insults and abuse come before bloodshed. Jesus traces murder back to anger and insult (Matthew 5:21-22), and James says the tongue sets the whole course of life on fire (James 3:6). Ben Sira's lesson for friendship: stop the insults before they become blows.

a: Who will post a guard at my mouth
p: The prayer begins with Psalm 141:3; 'Who will ...?' is a Hebrew way of saying 'If only ...!'
b: "LORD, post a guard for my mouth; / stand watch over the door of my lips" (Psalm 141:3). Ben Sira turns the psalm into a question, tis dōsei, "who will give", the Greek for the Hebrew mi yitten, which means "if only" (as in Deuteronomy 5:29). The answer comes in 23:1: the Lord, Father and Master of my life. The "seal" is the kind pressed on a closed document, so that it cannot be opened.

p: Ben Sira prays to God as his own Father, a rare form of address before the New Testament.
b: The Hebrew Bible calls God the Father of Israel (Isaiah 63:16; 64:8) and of the king (Psalm 89:26), but an individual's prayer to God as "Father" is rare before the New Testament. Ben Sira does it twice here (23:1, 4), and in 51:10 the Greek reads "I called on the Lord, the father of my lord". Wisdom 14:3 also prays "your providence, Father". Jesus teaches his disciples to pray "Our Father, who is in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). The Hebrew of 23:1-6 is lost, so the original wording is not known.

a: the wrongs I do without knowing
p: The Greek agnoēma is the word Hebrews uses for the sins the high priest atoned for.
b: Agnoēmata are wrongs done without knowing, the sins "by mistake" of Leviticus 4:2. Hebrews says the high priest's blood was offered "for himself and for the sins the people committed in ignorance" (Hebrews 9:7). Ben Sira asks God for whips over his thoughts so that even these will not go unchecked: he wants to be disciplined now rather than to fall later (23:3). Proverbs 3:11-12 calls such discipline the love of a father, which fits the address "Father".

p: Literally 'a lifting up of eyes': pride, or a roving eye. The next verses point to desire.
b: Meteōrismos ophthalmōn is a raising of the eyes. Proverbs lists "eyes held high" among the things the LORD hates (Proverbs 6:17), meaning pride, and the KJV here has "a proud look". But 23:5-6 go on to desire, gluttony and sexual lust, so the phrase may mean eyes that wander after what they want. Both senses fit a prayer about the senses that lead a man astray.

a: Listen, children, to discipline for the mouth
p: Codex Vaticanus heads this section 'Discipline for the mouth'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus lack the title.
b: Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, begins 23:7 with the title Paideia stomatos, "Discipline for the mouth", and then repeats the words in the sentence. Swete's notes report that Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus leave the title out. The Plain shows it as the heading. The section that follows (23:7-15) covers oaths, careless use of God's name, coarse talk and insults.

t: Left behind by his own lips
p: The Greek verb means 'be left behind'; the sense is 'be caught' or 'be stranded'.
b: Kataleiphthēsetai is "will be left behind". Joined to the last words of 23:7, "by his own lips", it means the sinner's own talk leaves him stranded, caught with no escape, the opposite of the man in 23:7 who "will not be trapped". The longer Greek has "In his folly the sinner will be left behind", which the KJV follows: "The sinner shall be left in his foolishness" (see the variant).

t: Oaths and the name of God
p: Ben Sira warns against the habit of swearing; Jesus and James go further.
b: Ben Sira does not forbid all oaths. He warns against the habit (23:9, 13), against careless use of God's name (Exodus 20:7) and against swearing "for nothing" (23:11). Jesus says, "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), and James repeats it (James 5:12). Whether Christians may swear oaths, for example in court, is a question the churches answer differently; the card on Matthew 5 sets out their views.

p: In the Greek and Roman world, a slave's testimony was taken under torture.
b: Exetazomenos endelechōs, "examined continually". A slave under examination was beaten, and the bruises never healed. The Roman commander in Acts orders the same for Paul: "to get the truth out of him under the whip" (Acts 22:24), with a related verb. Ben Sira's comparison: a man who keeps swearing by God's name cannot stay clean, any more than a slave who is always being flogged can stay unbruised.

a: the lash will never go away from his house
p: Genizah MS C has the Hebrew of this line: 'guilt' and 'the plague'.
b: Genizah MS C reads, "A man of oaths will be filled with guilt, and the plague (hannega') will not depart from his house." The Greek has "lawlessness" for "guilt" and mastix, "whip, scourge", for "plague". Mastix can also mean an affliction from God, as in Mark 5:29 ("cured of her affliction"). The rest of the verse explains: an oath broken through carelessness is sin, ignoring it doubles the sin, and a false oath brings trouble on the whole house (Zechariah 5:3-4).

p: Probably blasphemy, which the law punished by death; other readings are possible.
b: Lexis antiperibeblēmenē thanatō, "speech clothed around with death". Most readers take it to be blasphemy, the misuse of God's name, for which the law prescribed death: "Whoever speaks the name of the LORD with contempt must be put to death" (Leviticus 24:16). Coming after the oaths of 23:9-11, it may also mean false swearing. Some link it to 23:14, cursing one's parents, also a capital crime (Exodus 21:17). "Jacob's heritage" is Israel, the people God made his own.

a: Keep your father and mother in mind
t: Remember your parents among the great
p: Recalling your upbringing keeps you from coarse habits in high company.
b: Ben Sira imagines the pupil grown up and sitting in council with important people. If he has let crude talk become a habit, it will slip out there, and he will be shamed. Remembering his parents, the teaching they gave and the honor he owes them (Exodus 20:12; 3:1-16), will keep him careful. The curse on his birthday echoes Job and Jeremiah: "Cursed is the day / on which I was born" (Jeremiah 20:14; compare Job 3:3).

a: Two kinds of people pile up sins
p: Ben Sira uses the 'two, and a third' pattern of Proverbs and Amos.
b: Number sayings like "Here are three that are never full, / four that never say, 'Plenty!'" (Proverbs 30:15) build to a climax. Ben Sira's "two ... and the third" names the hot-tempered soul and the sexually immoral man, and the third, the worst, is the adulterer of 23:18-21, who brings on God's anger. Ben Sira uses the form again at 25:1-2, 7 and 26:5, 28.

a: in the body of his own flesh
p: Possibly incest with a close relative, or sexual sin with his own body.
b: En sōmati sarkos autou. "Flesh" in Hebrew and Greek can mean a blood relative, as in "any close relative of his own flesh" (Leviticus 18:6), so the line may describe incest. It may also mean simply that the man sins with his own body (compare 1 Corinthians 6:18), or that he cannot stop his body's craving. The fire of the last line is the burning of lust that consumes the one who feeds it.

p: Proverbs' stolen bread: forbidden pleasure always seems sweet.
b: Woman Folly in Proverbs says, "Water you steal tastes sweet, / and bread from hiding places is a delight" (Proverbs 9:17). Bread is linked with sexual sin in Proverbs too: "A prostitute may cost a round of bread" (Proverbs 6:26). For the immoral man, any woman will do, and he never tires of it until he dies.

p: The adulterer's question is asked by sinners throughout the Bible.
b: Job describes the adulterer who waits for dark: "'No eye will catch me,' he says" (Job 24:15). Isaiah mocks those who say, "Who sees us? Who is aware of us?" (Isaiah 29:15), and the Psalms the wicked who say God does not see (Psalm 94:7; Psalm 10:11). Ben Sira already warned against such talk in 16:17. The answer comes in 23:19-20: God's eyes see everything.

a: ten thousand times brighter than the sun
p: God's eyes outshine the sun and see into every hidden place.
b: "In every place the LORD has his eyes open, / on the lookout over evil people and good" (Proverbs 15:3). Ben Sira adds the picture of light: the adulterer hides in darkness, but God's eyes are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, and "darkness itself is not too dark for you" (Psalm 139:12). Hebrews says, "Not one created thing is out of his sight" (Hebrews 4:13).

a: Before all things were created, they were known to him
p: God knew everything before creation; Ben Sira still holds people responsible.
b: Ben Sira states God's knowledge of all things before they existed, as Isaiah does: "From the beginning I announce the end" (Isaiah 46:10; compare Psalm 139:16). Yet the same book insists that people choose freely and cannot blame God (15:11-20). Jewish and Christian teachers have held both together in different ways; the questions of predestination and free will are taken up on the free-will topic page. Here the point is moral: the adulterer cannot hide from a God who knew him before the world began.

a: This man will be punished in the city squares
p: Ben Sira punishes both; the law of Moses called for death for both.
b: The law says "the man and the woman who commit adultery" must be put to death (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). Ben Sira gives the man four verses (23:18-21) and the woman five (23:22-26), and he names no court penalty for either: the man is punished "in the city squares", publicly, and the woman is brought before the assembly. He agrees with the law that both are guilty, but he dwells longer on the woman's wrong, because of the children and the inheritance. Jesus sets both under the same judgment and adds the lustful look (Matthew 5:27-28).

a: she has refused to obey the Most High's law
p: Against God's law, against her husband and against his family line.
b: Ben Sira counts three wrongs: she broke God's law (Exodus 20:14), she wronged her husband, and she gave him heirs who are not his, which corrupts the family's inheritance. Proverbs says of the strange woman, "the covenant of her God has slipped from her mind" (Proverbs 2:17), so marriage is a covenant made before God. The words en porneia emoicheuthē join the two Greek words for sexual sin, porneia and adultery.

a: She will be brought out before the assembly
p: A public hearing; compare the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
b: The assembly, ekklēsia, is the gathering that judged public cases (21:17; Proverbs 5:14). In Ezekiel's allegory an unfaithful wife is judged before a crowd (Ezekiel 16:38-40). In John's Gospel the scribes and Pharisees "led in a woman caught in adultery. They stood her where everyone could see her" (John 8:3). "A reckoning" translates episkopē, a visit, an inquiry, or a punishment: her children's status will be examined.

a: Her children will not spread out roots
p: Like Wisdom 3:16, Ben Sira says such children will not thrive; Ezekiel 18 limits guilt to the sinner.
b: Wisdom of Solomon says the same: "adulterers' children will never reach full growth" (Wisdom 3:16), and "they will not send roots down deep" (Wisdom 4:3). Deuteronomy 23:2 bars one "born of a forbidden union" from the assembly. But the prophets insist that "A son will not bear the guilt of his father" (Ezekiel 18:20), and Jesus refuses to blame a man's parents for his blindness (John 9:3). Ben Sira may be describing the shame such children met in his society rather than God's judgment on them; read as a judgment, his words stand in tension with Ezekiel 18 and Deuteronomy 24:16.
r: Wisdom 3:16-19; Wisdom 4:3-6; Deuteronomy 23:2; Ezekiel 18:20; Deuteronomy 24:16; John 9:3

a: her disgrace will not be rubbed out
p: Ben Sira echoes Proverbs 6:33 on the adulterer's lasting shame.
b: Proverbs says of the man who commits adultery, "Beatings and shame are what he will find, / and his disgrace will not be rubbed out" (Proverbs 6:33). Ben Sira applies the same words to the woman. The Plain uses Proverbs' English so the link shows.

p: The end of the section returns to the fear of the Lord, as the Psalms praise the sweetness of God's law.
b: Stolen bread seemed sweet to the immoral man (23:17); the true sweetness is God's commandments: "they are sweeter than honey, / than what drips from the comb" (Psalm 19:10). Those "left behind", the community that has seen the adulterers' end, learn the lesson of the whole section. The verse closes chapters 19-23 with the theme of 19:20 and 21:11: nothing is better than the fear of the Lord.
